content: Ensuring HIV testing is conducted according to national guidelines is critical. This process should include counseling and a clear pathway to confirmatory HIV testing and treatment for individuals who test reactive (positive) while using the dapivirine vaginal ring. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that HIV testing for dapivirine ring users follow the same strategy and algorithm as for other individuals. Introducing more expensive or complex testing methods may limit access and is unlikely to provide additional benefits in settings where nucleic acid testing (NAT) or fourth-generation serology assays are not routinely used for HIV diagnosis. Adherence support should be a central component of service delivery. Flexible and personalized support is particularly important as women begin using this new product. Frequent check-ins with healthcare or lay providers may be necessary to assist women during the initial stages of use. Younger women may require additional adherence support, and partner or peer support should also be considered. Demand Creation The dapivirine vaginal ring is a novel product. In communities where women face a high risk of HIV but have little or no experience with vaginal ring products (e.g., contraceptive vaginal rings), awareness programs for both the community and healthcare providers should be developed and implemented before and during the product's introduction. These programs should engage women’s networks and key population groups to address concerns and answer questions about the product. Messaging for men and male partners should also be included, as some women have reported that discussing ring use with their partners was supportive and helpful in maintaining use. Training and Support for Providers In high HIV-burden settings considering the introduction of the dapivirine vaginal ring, healthcare providers are unlikely to have prior experience with vaginal ring products. Addressing provider concerns and issues will be essential for successful implementation. Research Gaps Safety in Pregnancy and Breastfeeding The monthly use of the dapivirine vaginal ring has been shown to be safe and effective for HIV prevention in non-pregnant women of childbearing potential. However, data on its effects during pregnancy and on infants are limited. Animal studies using high concentrations of dapivirine vaginal gel have not identified adverse effects on maternal health or fetal development. In the MTN-020/ASPIRE trial, 169 of 2,629 women became pregnant, and no adverse effects on pregnancy or infant outcomes were observed during the periconception period. Nevertheless, further safety studies are needed to evaluate the use of the dapivirine vaginal ring during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Ongoing studies, such as MTN-042 (DELIVER) and MTN-043 (B-PROTECTED), are expected to provide additional safety data. Effectiveness in Women Younger Than 21 Years A subanalysis of women under 21 years of age did not demonstrate efficacy in this group, and adherence to the product was low. Current studies, such as MTN-034 (REACH), aim to assess adherence, safety, and barriers to use in this age group, as well as strategies to support adherence and continuation. Acceptability Among Key Population Groups No research has yet been conducted on implementing the dapivirine vaginal ring among key populations, such as sex workers and women who use drugs. Conducting surveys to understand the values and preferences of these groups will be important. If these communities view the ring as a valuable HIV prevention option, their involvement in program design and development will be critical. Combination Prevention Women should be counseled on the dapivirine vaginal ring alongside other prevention options, such as daily oral PrEP, male and female condoms, and partner services. Some women may switch between oral PrEP and the vaginal ring or use both simultaneously. While using both products together is likely safe, there is no evidence of additional benefit from combined use. Adherence to either method is crucial for optimal protection. Further research is needed to understand patterns of use, including intermittent use of the ring or switching between prevention methods. Cost and Cost-Effectiveness Both oral PrEP and the dapivirine vaginal ring are costly prevention interventions. WHO recommends prioritizing these options for women at substantial risk of HIV, as their use is likely to provide the greatest benefit and cost-effectiveness. Further cost-effectiveness analyses using real-world data across various settings and populations would help guide future implementation for maximum impact. For adults and adolescents, the recommended backbone regimen is tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) with lamivudine (3TC) or emtricitabine (FTC), combined with dolutegravir (DTG) as the preferred third drug. Alternative third drugs, such as atazanavir/ritonavir (ATV/r), darunavir/ritonavir (DRV/r), lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r), or raltegravir (RAL), may be considered when DTG is unavailable. For children under 10 years, zidovudine (AZT) with 3TC is the preferred backbone regimen, with DTG as the preferred third drug when approved dosing is available.g., tears, non-blood-stained saliva, urine, or sweat). Infant Prophylaxis Infants born to mothers with HIV who are at high risk of acquiring HIV should receive dual prophylaxis with daily AZT and nevirapine (NVP) for the first six weeks of life. Breastfed infants at high risk should continue prophylaxis for an additional six weeks, using either AZT and NVP or NVP alone. Infants of mothers receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART) and breastfeeding should receive six weeks of daily NVP. Enhanced postnatal prophylaxis is recommended for high-risk infants, particularly in settings with high HIV prevalence. Addressing Vertical Transmission Despite progress in reducing mother-to-child transmission, challenges remain in retaining women living with HIV in healthcare services and ensuring effective ART during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Enhanced infant prophylaxis is critical for infants born to mothers who did not receive early, effective ART. WHO guidelines recommend dual-drug prophylaxis for high-risk infants, which can be extended for up to 12 weeks for breastfeeding infants. Implementation Considerations Improving uptake and completion rates for HIV PEP requires adherence support and providing a full 28-day course of medication at the first clinic visit. National programs should align PEP regimens with antiretroviral drugs already procured for HIV treatment and prevention.
